course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Consequences of Industrialization
unit.description: Study why industrial states built empires, how colonized peoples resisted, how economies were reshaped, and why millions of people migrated.

topic.title: Effects of Migration
topic.summary: How migrants formed ethnic enclaves, how migration changed home societies, and how some receiving societies responded with exclusion.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.7 key concept: receiving societies did not always embrace immigrants, as seen in the Chinese Exclusion Act and the White Australia Policy
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing anti-immigrant laws in the United States and Australia, 1882–1901
stimulusBlocks.text:
Chinese workers helped build the western United States, including the transcontinental railroad completed in 1869. As jobs grew scarce in the 1870s, some white workers and politicians blamed Chinese immigrants. In 1882 Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, which banned Chinese laborers from entering the country.

In 1901, the new nation of Australia passed laws designed to keep out non-European immigrants, a set of policies known as the White Australia Policy. Both measures reflected nativism and racial ideas of the time.

Both restricted it.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.7 key concept: migrants often created ethnic enclaves, and migration affected gender roles in home societies
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the effects of migration on communities, 1850–1914
stimulusBlocks.text:
Migrants often settled together in ethnic enclaves, where they could speak their own language, worship in familiar ways, and help each other find work. Chinese communities grew in Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and San Francisco, and Indian communities grew in East Africa and the Caribbean.

Migration also changed the societies migrants left. Most migrants were young men. In southern Italy and southern China, women often took on more responsibility for farms and family businesses while men worked abroad and sent money home.

Their work increased.
Women took on more responsibility while men worked abroad.

questions.prompt: Which detail shows how Chinese immigrants responded to discrimination?
choices: They returned to China in large numbers after 1882
They won the right to vote in California in the 1870s
They left railroad work to search for gold in the Sierra Nevada mountains
They formed associations that gave credit, housing, and aid
questions.explanation: Community associations supported newcomers who faced hostility and low wages.
choiceExplanations: The passage does not describe a mass return in 1882.
The passage describes exclusion, not voting rights.
Many worked in gold mines and railroads at the same time, and the passage describes no change from railroad to mining work.
Community associations supported newcomers who faced hostility and low wages.
questions.distinguisher: Some Chinese immigrants did return home, but the passage's example of response is organization within the United States.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.7 key concept: migrants formed enclaves, and nativist reactions led to restrictions on immigration
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Chinese immigration to the United States, 1850–1943
stimulusBlocks.text:
Between 1850 and 1882, roughly 300,000 Chinese migrants came to the United States, many to work in California gold mines and to build the Central Pacific Railroad. Facing low wages and hostility from white workers, many Chinese formed their own neighborhoods with associations that provided credit, housing, and aid.

In the 1870s an economic depression increased anti-Chinese violence, and in 1882 Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, which banned the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years. The law was renewed and made permanent in 1902 and stayed in force until 1943.

questions.prompt: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was most directly a response to
choices: pressure from the Chinese government to stop emigration to America
a shortage of laborers needed to finish the railroads
a treaty with Britain that limited migration from Asia
competition for jobs and racial prejudice in a depression
questions.explanation: The passage links the law to the economic depression of the 1870s and anti-Chinese violence.
choiceExplanations: The Qing government did not ask for exclusion.
Exclusion came after the Central Pacific Railroad was finished.
The law was passed by Congress and not tied to a treaty with Britain.
The passage links the law to the economic depression of the 1870s and anti-Chinese violence.
questions.distinguisher: Railroad construction had drawn Chinese workers earlier, but the law followed the end of that demand.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many Chinese migrants went to California in the 1850s and 1860s?
choices: Indenture contracts bound most of them to plantation work
The Qing government sent settlers to claim land in America
Gold mining and railroad building offered work and wages
The Chinese Exclusion Act guaranteed them jobs and land
questions.explanation: The gold rush and the Central Pacific Railroad drew workers seeking wages higher than they could earn at home.
choiceExplanations: Indenture bound many Chinese and Indian migrants in the Caribbean and Peru, but most Chinese in California came on credit, not plantation contracts.
The Qing government discouraged emigration and did not send settlers.
The gold rush and the Central Pacific Railroad drew workers seeking wages higher than they could earn at home.
The 1882 act barred Chinese laborers; it did not invite them.
questions.distinguisher: Indentured labor was common elsewhere in the Americas, but Chinese migrants in California mostly worked for wages.
